A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, and their supplied text, equations and displays are readable. However, v2 ends after its references despite citing absent appendices; v3 includes Appendices A–N. Earlier supplementary contents cannot be checked, so appendix differences below concern newly supplied documentation and evidence, not necessarily newly performed experiments.

before.justification: Sections 4.2–4.4 report original extraction results, training and fusion ablations, interferer-duration tests, and a ten-user enrollment-labeling experiment.

after.justification: V3 retains original experimental results and additionally supplies real-recording listener ratings, cross-dataset evaluations, robustness analyses and failure cases.

M1.justification: The Siamese TF-GridNet encoders, self-attention fusion, pooling size 40, causal extraction branch and two-stage losses remain unchanged. New pseudocode, binaural input details and clean-enrollment handling document components or applications already described or referenced in v2; they do not establish an algorithm revision.

E1.justification: V3 adds evaluated natural recordings from Freesound and VoxConverse, MSDWild/VoxConverse speech-overlap analysis, and WSJ0 extraction tests. Its appendices also document broader enrollment-quality, duration and interferer conditions. LibriSpeech, WHAM! and the four binaural-RIR sources remain; some supplementary scenarios were already mentioned in v2 without supplied evidence.

E2.justification: Main Table 1 replaces SpeakerBeam with USEF-TFGridnet, while NMF, TCE and the binaural LookOnceToHear comparison remain. SpeakerBeam is still evaluated as TD-SpeakerBeam in Appendix J, so it is not removed from the entire paper. The new MOS comparison also includes unprocessed audio.

E3.justification: Tables 1–2 add PESQ and WER to the four original metrics. The new listening study uses five recordings, ten participants and a 1–4 rating scale. Appendices supply pooling, enrollment-quality, transfer and confusion-testing protocols. The existing main evaluation retains 5000 test-clean samples; newly disclosed training settings do not establish changes to those experiments.

E4.justification: The original training/fusion ablations, interferer-duration tests and labeling-robustness study remain. V3 supplies extensive additional evidence on pooling, individual interferer types, enrollment length and quality, speaker confusion, WSJ0 fine-tuning, and successful/failing extractions. Several analyses were only cross-referenced in v2. Redisplaying the labeling study as Table 3 is not itself a new analysis.

E5.justification: Table 3 replaces labeling-study boxplots with numerical plus/minus summaries, and Tables 6–7 specify averaging inference timings over 50 repetitions. Cross-sample standard deviations and the main comparison's two-sample t-tests at 90% confidence remain. No increase in training-run or seed replication is established.

E6.justification: The original four metrics for retained methods match across v2 Table 1 and v3 Tables 1–2, including the proposed model's 8.85 dB SI-SNRi for two-speaker mixtures and enrollments. V3 adds USEF and PESQ/WER entries, extensive appendix results, and MOS scores of 3.35 for ours, 2.60 for FiLM, 1.45 for USEF and 2.10 for unprocessed audio. These are added findings, not a same-setting improvement by the revised model.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(3), the independently timed speech assumption and the formal interferer categories remain unchanged. Appendix A supplies empirical overlap statistics, and Appendix K uses cosine similarity for error analysis; neither introduces a new proof, theorem or substantively revised formal model.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions and conclusion retain the same enrollment strategy, two-stage training contribution, over-2.1 dB SI-SNRi advantage and 60% reduction in optimization steps. Additional experiments support these retained claims without redefining their scientific scope.

C2.justification: V3 expands interpretations of pooling trade-offs, different sensitivity to positive versus negative interferers, weak-enrollment limitations and mixed benefits from WSJ0 fine-tuning. Appendices explain clean-enrollment normalization failure, speaker confusion, omitted target speech and interfering-speech leakage. The original limitations concerning distillation, artifacts and clean-enrollment performance remain.

D1.justification: Appendices B–C supply previously unavailable data-generation and split details, VAD processing, STFT/network parameters, optimization schedules, batch size, 200k/400k training-stage budgets, and baseline adaptations/fine-tuning. V3 also explains binaural input representation and clean-enrollment preprocessing, and adds an implementation link. These are predominantly new disclosures rather than demonstrated changes to existing settings.

R1.justification: Section 2 and the original 37 references are retained. V3 adds references for WebRTC VAD, MOCOv3-related training motivation and target-speaker confusion analysis. USEF-TSE was already cited in v2. The broader research positioning and novelty argument remain stable.

P1.justification: The main section order, related work and conclusion remain stable. Rewriting is concentrated in the encoder-fusion explanation and convergence discussion, with additional explanatory paragraphs, an appendix outline and updated affiliation/contact/conference text. Most expansion supplies scientific documentation rather than extensively rewriting existing prose.

P2.justification: V3 redraws Figure 2, adds fusion pseudocode, splits the main results table into monaural and binaural tables with additional metric rows, and replaces the labeling boxplot with Table 3. New MOS and appendix tables, quality plots and waveform/spectrogram examples substantially expand the displays. New inconsistencies include duplicate Figure 4 labels and an SI-SDRi caption on the MOS table.

improvement.justification: V3 supplies substantial implementation details and supplementary evidence that v2 merely referenced, resolving important reproducibility and evidential gaps. Real-recording evaluations, WSJ0 tests and failure analyses make practical applicability and limitations more assessable. The small MOS study and inconsistent captions and metric descriptions weaken parts of the additions, but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in documented evidence and technical transparency.
